To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the mandibular division innervates the ipsilateral trigeminal motor nucleus and the ipsilateral cerebel-lum and that the contralateral dorsal horn is innervated by a crossed trigeminal aﬀerent projection.

primary trigeminal aferents project bilateraly to dorsal horn and cerebellum, ipsilaterally to cuneate, supratrigeminall and vagal nuclei and reticular formation, as well as to the ipsilateral and contralateral dorsal horn.

the trigeminal primary aferents project bilateraly to the dorsal horn and ipslaterally to the cerebellum, the reticular formation and the cuneate, the solitary, the supratrigemina and the vagal nuclei.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the distribution of the primary afferent fibers of the mandibulary division of the rat’s trigeminal nerve.
the distribution of primary afferent fibers from the mandibular branch of the trigemial nerve in the dorsal brain stem of the rat.
the central projections of trigeminal primary aferents.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the trigeminal primary aferents are distributed bilaterally to the ipsilateral trigeminal sensory nuclei and the contralateral trigeminal nuclei, and bilaterally to all other nuclei in the brainstem and spinal cord.

primary afferents from the mandibular division are widely distributed throughout the brainstem, and project to all known sensory relay nuclei, and also to the motor and autonomic nuclei of the trigemina, and to the cerebellum.

primary afferent fibers from the trigeminal nerve terminate on the contralateral side in the dorsal horn and on the ipsilateral side in the ipsilateral dorsal horn, cerebellum, cuneate and supratrigemina nuclei and the reticular formation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
all the major brainstem sensory nuclei receive a direct projection from primary trigeminal aﬀerents.

primary afferents of the trigemimal ganglion project bilaterally throughout the medullary dorsal horn and ipsilateral throughout the cerebellar cortex, parafloccular cortex, reticular formation and the cuneate, dorsal motor vagal and solitary, supratigeminal and vagus nuclei.

all the known primary afferents projections to the brainstem were labeled when the trigeminal nerve was transected, and that all these projections were also labeled by application of HRP to each of the sensory branches of the nerve.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there are more connections between the trigeminal nerve and the central nervous system than was previously appreciated.
the trigeminal primary aferents are not restricted to the brainstem trigeminothalamic system, but project to the ipsilateral cerebelom, and to many brainstem nuclei.
the primary trigeminal aferents project widely to the brainstem and spinal cord.
